brief.head: No face, no brand
brief.text: Perun sells no brand and no credentials, only the quality of his argument, Ajay Shah said. He called him “the repudiation of credentialism”. {031-C01}

brief.head: Young nation, old army
brief.text: US Marines average 21 to 25 years old, Amit Varma said, relaying Perun; India’s army averages 32 to 34, because soldiering is treated as a career. {031-C10}

brief.head: Uber for artillery
brief.text: When the war began, Ukrainians built an Uber for artillery, Amit Varma recalled. Small, empowered, even subversive teams like that, Ajay Shah said, are what armies need. {031-J19}

brief.head: Four wars, no passport
brief.text: France and Germany killed each other from the Napoleonic Wars to 1945, Ajay Shah said. Now people live in France and drive to work in Germany, showing no passport. {031-S10}

brief.head: Sukhoi surplus
brief.text: A tidbit from Perun’s video, as Amit Varma relayed it: there are more Sukhoi-30s flying over India than over Russia. {#sukhoi}

thought.text: First comes the ideas. After that there is a possibility of implementation.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, finding hope in a new generation of Indian thinkers

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what ails India’s military
lead.head: Brains wanted at the front
body: Ajay Shah set Amit Varma some homework: a YouTube video on Indian defence by Perun, a pseudonymous economist who talks over PowerPoint slides. Varma, who has done several episodes on the subject, could not find a single elementary error. {031-S02}
The video became the launch pad for a long conversation about what is wrong with India’s armed forces and how to fix it. Shah’s answer, again and again, was that a modern military runs on brains.
“Wars are won by thinking, by cleverness, by creativity, by flexibility, by teamwork,” he said.
The macho image of the army, all blood-curdling screams, is a recent populist turn, he argued. The army of Sam Manekshaw, Y. B. Chavan and Indira Gandhi in 1971 was quiet, clinical and professional.
## Where the money goes

Varma relayed Perun’s numbers. The United States spends about ten times as much as India on defence, and China about five times. Of India’s budget, 53 per cent goes on salaries and pensions. {031-C09}

Shah stepped back to first principles. Strategy, he said, has three steps: list the threats, design a force that meets them cost-efficiently, and move towards it step by step from where you are. {031-C03}
India’s officials rarely think that far ahead. They “play for their time on the watch”, he said: a person promoted at 59 plays for one year.
Nor is the trouble unique to defence. Hiring, contracting, budgeting and checks on coercive power break down in health and finance too, Shah said, and specialists in their silos never see it.
## The prescription

Shah’s remedies began outside the barracks. Diplomacy is the outer layer, he said, and war is what happens when it fails. A country that opens with “strategic autonomy”, he argued, has taken its domestic policy off the negotiating table. {031-C07}

Only the United States, he said, can build frontier weapons alone at a sensible cost. India’s attempts, the Arjun tank and the Light Combat Aircraft, show what going it alone produces: equipment that arrives 20 years late.

A poor country should aim one notch behind the frontier, buy fewer types of equipment, and get unit costs down through scale. And it should hire for brainpower, because fitness can be trained and brains cannot.
His boldest idea was a new army beside the old: small formations of about a thousand people with modern manuals, woven into the Air Force and Navy, while the old army slowly shrinks.
## The long game
Varma’s thoughts, he said, were “all pessimistic”: bad incentives, organisations too ossified to change, and too little intellectual capacity in the state.
Shah added a darker one. Defeat used to force reform: the loss to China in 1962 led to army reforms that paid off in 1965 and 1971.
Nuclear deterrence has largely ended such wars between India, China and Pakistan, he said, so weaknesses may be piling up unseen. {031-C14}

Yet Shah called himself fundamentally optimistic. For the first time, he said, India is building a literature, and a new generation of people who understand law, public administration and state capacity.
Varma had a rejoinder. “Both of us are playing a long game,” he said, “but as your hero John Maynard Keynes once said, in the long run, we are all dead.”

second.label: Army and society
second.head: Corps values
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how German veterans fed Nazism, and the road Nehru chose
body: After the First World War, Ajay Shah said, German veterans came back into an informal organisation called the Free Corps. It became home to toxic right-wing nationalism: strongman values, intolerance and a willingness to take to the streets. {#freecorps}

That was the raw material around which the Nazi Party was built, and many brownshirts came from the Free Corps. Hitler’s society then fed back into a military project to conquer the whole world. It worked out very badly for Germany.

India, Shah argued, took the other road: keeping the army in its barracks, professional and out of politics, was one of Nehru’s great achievements. {031-S08} Amit Varma pointed to Pakistan, where the military came to dominate society.

quote.text: It is one of the great achievements of Nehru that the institutional arrangements were made to keep the army in their barracks

third.head: Chess, poker, then biceps
body: Ajay Shah gets very depressed by newspaper reports on how the Indian military hires. Thousands of young men gather at one village and run 15 kilometres, and roughly the fastest one per cent are shortlisted. {031-S12}
“You could take almost any person and train them to military levels of fitness,” he said. “You cannot take almost any person and train them to military level of brain power.” {031-C11}
He wants “Vaishnav levels of brain power in the military”, naming the episode’s cameraman, Vaishnav Vyas. “He’s a wimp, he doesn’t have any biceps,” Shah said. “Adding biceps is trivial.” {031-J07}

Paper one of his recruitment exam: an Elo rating on chess.com. Paper two: poker, because in military affairs the board is not visible. Ukraine’s army, he added, is 10 per cent women, who make great snipers. {#women}

sections.label: Perun’s diagnosis
sections.head: Four horsemen of procurement
sections.caption: Perun’s case against Indian defence
body: Perun’s starting point, as Amit Varma summarised it, is that India is not technologically backward. It ran the Chandrayaan mission for a fraction of what other space programmes cost, and it is a nuclear power. Its armed forces are another story.
India did not have to build an army from scratch. It inherited its share of the British Indian Army. Then, as Varma relayed Perun’s dry humour, “the guns immediately turned at each other.” {031-J04}
Asked whose side India is on, especially over the Russia-Ukraine war, Perun has a ready answer: “India is on India’s side.”
## A beast with old weapons
The Navy and the Air Force, Varma said, are relatively advanced and evolving quickly. The army is 1.2 million people. {#army} It is, he said, “a beast with really old weaponry”.

The money goes on people. Pensions took 12 per cent of the budget in 2008 and take 23 per cent now. Of roughly $47 billion in 2023, only about $3.7 billion went on modernising the force, though Varma warned that some figures might be slightly off. {031-C09}

~ The Agnipath scheme tried to change this, starting everyone on a five-year contract. {#agnipath} Those not kept on got a one-time tax-free severance instead of pensions, and the scheme set off protests across the country, because Indians think of the army as a job for life.

quote.text: Fifty-three percent of that goes into salaries and pensions, of which pensions alone account for 23%.

sections.label: Strategy
sections.head: First, list the threats
sections.caption: the three steps of military strategy
body: Ajay Shah set out military strategy in three steps. First, write down the threats, which change: China’s economy is now five times the size of India’s. Second, design a force that meets those threats cost-efficiently. Third, move towards it.

He wanted “cost efficient” in bold: with infinite artillery you can win every battle, but nobody has it. India spends about 2.5 per cent of GDP on its military, perhaps half a per cent on equipment. {#gdp}

Weapons last about 20 years, so replacing everything at once is out of reach: “nobody’s going to give you that money.” Instead, re-engineer old T-72 and T-90 tanks with new weapons and electronics. {031-C03}
## Playing for one year
Amit Varma raised the MiG-21, an aircraft of the 1960s that India should have stopped using 30 years ago. Search for MiG-21 crashes, he said, and you find experienced pilots dying in them. {031-S04}

Shah traced it to a failure across Indian government: the inability to think strategically. Officials plan for their own tenure, he said; promoted at 59, they play for one year. {031-C04} In Britain, the US and Germany, security communities outlast elections and own the 25-year view.

~ Under Narasimha Rao, Vajpayee and Jaswant Singh, after the Soviet Union collapsed, India began to rethink its alignments. Shah judges the effort incomplete: a pro-Soviet, pro-Russian strain of thinking persists.

quote.text: Identify your threats, dream of what is an appropriate force design, and then do that incremental process of evolution given where you are

sections.label: Foundations
sections.head: The same plumbing, everywhere
sections.caption: the four foundational processes
body: A health-expert friend of Ajay Shah’s believed for years that Indian healthcare worked badly because economists kept the best people in finance. It took him years to persuade her that finance has huge problems too. {031-S07}

The same failures, Shah said, run through health, finance, defence, intelligence and monetary policy. {031-C05} In *In Service of the Republic*, he and Vijay Kelkar call them foundational processes: HR, government contracting, budgeting and finance, and checks and balances on coercive power.

Specialists miss this because they stay in their silos, and in health they narrow further, to polio or HIV. They also treat the plumbing as beyond their pay grade. A military officer cannot change the General Financial Rules that govern contracting.
## Two jobs, done well

Early European states, Shah said, did only two things: raise taxes and wage wars. {031-C06} They ran no ordnance factories. Arms came from private vendors and mercenaries, who even sold arms to Indian kings, so states had to learn to contract.
India did it upside down. Among the poorest and least capable states in the world, it expanded, “in a socialist frenzy”, into almost everything, and now does it all at small scale and badly.
~ Amit Varma drew the lesson in the show’s name. Everything is everything, he said: never let your vision get so compartmentalised that you miss the broader principles.

quote.text: So this verticalization, the compartmentalization, the disciplinary emphasis is the source of difficulty in thinking about Indian public policy.

sections.label: Diplomacy first
sections.head: The big stick, used sparingly
sections.caption: diplomacy as defence’s outer layer
body: Amit Varma began with the military theorist Clausewitz, “war is politics by other means”, and added a twist: “which means if you’re doing politics well, you don’t need the war.” {031-J16}

Ajay Shah took up the theme. Military power is the big stick a country must have and should use as little as possible, because it is very expensive and because killing people is always morally wrong. When war comes, he said, diplomacy has failed, as it did before the First World War and before Putin invaded Ukraine.

In 1947 India inherited a first-rate military: many of its officers had trained at Sandhurst. {#sandhurst} It inherited no foreign-policy capability, and its diplomats, Shah said, still make speeches and negotiate nothing.
## Dancing alone
Diplomacy means states changing their domestic policies to suit each other. Open with “strategic autonomy”, Shah said, and you declare yours off the table: “then very well, go dance alone.” {031-C07}

Treaties and coalitions let countries insure one another, which brings down defence costs. Taking on China alone, whose economy outweighs India’s much as Russia’s outweighs Ukraine’s, would be very expensive.

~ Shah even recast 1971. Indians blame the United States for backing Pakistan, he said, but that alignment was a failure of Indian foreign policy, and Bangladesh might have broken free without it. {031-S11}

quote.text: Killing less people is a very high virtue.

sections.label: Self-reliance
sections.head: Twenty years too late
sections.caption: why India cannot build alone
body: Ajay Shah can date the Light Combat Aircraft by his own education. When he started college in 1983, he benefited greatly from a computational fluid dynamics lab funded as part of the LCA project. {031-S05}

Build frontier equipment alone, he said, and you can spend decades on it, only to find the world has moved on. Of the Arjun tank and the LCA he said: “It’ll come 20 years late, but 20 years late it’ll be too late.”

Only one country builds such systems alone at a sensible cost: the United States. {031-C08} It has the deepest private ecosystem of defence research, funded through DARPA and others. It builds thousands of fighters, not hundreds. {#thousands} And it does not practise self-reliance: its contracts flow to Japan, Israel and Europe.
## Who sells the laser?

Everyone else works in partnership: Germany with Britain on a fighter, Korea with Poland, Japan with a whole array of countries. Supply chains also run through foreign policy. If a tank’s laser range finder comes from Sweden, Shah said, being prickly with Sweden puts it at risk.
~ He was also cool on India’s technical prowess. Most of the software done in India, he said, is pretty basic, and its engineering capabilities are relatively limited.

quote.text: There is only one country that is able to do isolated development of global state of the art systems at a half sensible cost.

sections.label: Defence economics
sections.head: Buy B-grade, buy in bulk
sections.caption: buying one notch behind the frontier
body: A poor country, Ajay Shah said, should aim one notch behind the global frontier. “I will not buy an F-35. I will buy a B-grade,” he said, and he would pass on the Abrams and Leopard tanks too.
Counting equipment misleads, he argued, like judging a chess position by adding up the pieces. In 1967 the Arabs vastly outgunned Israel, and Israel won the Six-Day War. {#israel}

Then comes scale: fewer types of equipment, integration into global supply chains, exports. A mix of Rafales, MiG-21s and Sukhois is “confused”, he said. “The core insight of the military industrial complex of the defence industrial base is scale.” {031-C12}
## A clean slate

Amit Varma doubted that the army could ever be cut down politically. Shah was unmoved: “This is a country where customs duties went from three fifty percent to fifteen percent. Anything is possible.” {031-J09}

Merging the Navy and Air Force into theatre commands now, he feared, would smother their better culture. Instead, copy Russia’s battalion tactical groups and start afresh, with modern manuals and processes, while the old army is phased out like an old pension system. {031-C13}
~ China’s PLA, he noted, once took in agricultural surplus labour much as India’s army does, then cut about half its personnel. {#pla}

quote.text: It’s a bad workman who blames his tools.

side.boxText: Perun is a pseudonymous economist on YouTube whose videos are PowerPoint slides crammed with words, with him talking over them. Amit Varma has never seen him on camera. He has about half a million subscribers, and many videos pass a million views. {#subs}

contQuote.text: So there is this feedback loop that you need to fail, and then enough people get kicked into action to undertake those difficult transformations. And this is a recurring theme all across the world of public policy.

stories.caption: the township that must fly to space
stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells Perun’s parable of Indian defence buying
stories.head: A township on a room’s budget
body: Imagine you are a foreign defence firm, Amit Varma said, and India comes to you with an order. {#township} He was retelling Perun’s case against Indian defence procurement in a metaphor of his own, conceding that Perun had probably put it better.
India gives you the budget for a single room. With it, you must build a super-advanced township, and make it fly to space.
There are conditions. You must work with an Indian partner and own only 49 per cent. You must transfer all your technology and know-how. If anything goes wrong, you bear 100 per cent of the blame.
And while all this is happening, the requirements may keep changing, “because somebody will think of something”.

Perun names four horsemen of the defence procurement apocalypse: budgets, requirements, demands for indigenisation and bureaucratic procedure. The requirements, a former defence minister said, according to Perun’s video, read like something “straight out of a Marvel Comics superhero movie”. {031-J05}
Perun’s summary, as Varma relayed it: the army asks for technology for 2030 and is told it can have technology from 2010. It refuses. “And we are still stuck with technology from 1940.” {031-S03}
This, as Perun says in the video, calls for a slow clap. It is, Varma added, a remarkably bad situation.
~ Later in the episode, Varma said Perun was hardly exaggerating. India still has MiG-21s flying overhead, he said, “and crashing, mind you”.
stories.why: When budgets are tiny, specifications fantastical, indigenisation forced and procedures tangled, the best vendors walk away. The buyer is left with the oldest equipment of all, the very opposite of what the army asked for.

stories.start: We had a moment where there was a negotiation in the early days
stories.end: the nightmare of OROP. It's the exact opposite of where we had begun
stories.caption: the military pension deal that vanished
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a pension reform agreed, then forgotten
stories.head: The pension deal that went AWOL
body: Early in the life of the National Pension System, S. Narayan of the Finance Ministry sent Ajay Shah to hold careful meetings with the Army, Navy and Air Force on bringing the NPS to the military. {#deputed} The senior leadership of all three agreed, orally. Shah did those negotiations himself.

Then the UPA came to power in 2004. The CPI(M) blocked the NPS for years, pensions moved, wrongly in Shah’s view, from the Department of Economic Affairs to the Department of Financial Services, and the institutional memory was lost.
By the time the NPS rolled out, the military connection was gone. “And today we are holding the nightmare of OROP,” Shah said. “It’s the exact opposite of where we had begun.” {031-S06}
~ It was, he said, an example of disciplinary boundaries interrupting the flow of knowledge.
stories.why: Reform agreements can quietly evaporate through changes of government and bureaucratic reshuffles. Here the result was One Rank One Pension, and pensions that now swallow so much of India’s defence budget.
stories.postscript: Pensions take 23 per cent of the defence budget, up from 12 per cent in 2008, by Perun’s figures as Varma relayed them.

stories.start: Look at what the Poles did. The Poles have purchased
stories.end: they get royalties on future sales of those Korean tanks all over the world
stories.caption: Poland’s Korean tank
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on buying one notch below the best
stories.head: Poles apart from self-reliance
body: Poland expects to be next if Ukraine falls, Ajay Shah said, and wants thousands of tanks ready for a Russian invasion. {031-S13}

It did not buy the German Leopard or the American Abrams. It bought a very good South Korean tank, a little behind those two, which fits the Polish budget. Then it signed deep contracts with the Koreans: partnering in research and manufacturing, taking equity, and earning royalties on future sales of those tanks all over the world.
“They didn’t say self-reliance,” Shah said. “They said, let’s be pragmatic.”
~ Korean carmakers already build cars in India, he noted. Korean tank-makers should think of doing the same, because it is cheaper, but India would then have to play for the world market.
stories.why: A country with limited money does better to buy one notch below the frontier, at scale and through partnerships, than to chase the best equipment or self-reliance. India, Shah argued, is such a country. {031-C12}

stories.start: And after Narsimarau died in the early two thousands, Vajpai told the story
stories.end: because I know this is good for the country
stories.caption: Rao’s handover to Vajpayee
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a handover between prime ministers
stories.head: The material is ready
body: After Narasimha Rao died, Amit Varma said, Atal Bihari Vajpayee told a story about 1996, when Rao handed power to him. Varma counts them as India’s two finest prime ministers.
Rao told him: “Saamagri taiyaar hai.” The material is ready; the nuclear tests can be carried out.

Rao had not carried out the tests himself, Varma said, because elections had brought in a new government, and as a matter of courtesy he left them to it. {031-S09} “We are lucky that they had that shared vision that they did.”

~ Manmohan Singh carried the turn away from the Soviet Union on. In UPA-1 he pushed the nuclear deal with the US despite the Left, even in his own party, and was ready to stop being prime minister over it.
stories.why: Strategic shifts survive changes of government when leaders across parties share a vision. Ajay Shah’s caveat: the realignment came from the top, from Rao, Vajpayee, Jaswant Singh and Manmohan Singh, not from the bureaucracy, and stayed incomplete. {#fromthetop}

quiz.q: What does Perun say when asked whose side India is on in the Russia-Ukraine war?
quiz.a: “India is on India’s side”, as Amit Varma relayed Perun’s dry humour.

quiz.q: What, by Perun’s count, are the four horsemen of the defence procurement apocalypse?
quiz.a: Low budgets, crazy requirements, demands for indigenisation, and bureaucratic procedure, as Varma relayed them.

quiz.q: Which two exams would Ajay Shah set for recruits to the Indian Army?
quiz.a: A chess.com Elo rating, then poker, because on a battlefield the board is hidden.

quiz.q: What did Narasimha Rao tell Vajpayee when he handed over power in 1996?
quiz.a: “Saamagri taiyaar hai”: the material is ready, the nuclear tests can go ahead.

quiz.q: Which tank did Poland choose to prepare for a possible Russian invasion, and why?
quiz.a: A very good South Korean tank, a notch below the best, that fits its budget.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, has the old loop of reform through defeat stopped working?
quiz.a: Nuclear deterrence between India, China and Pakistan has largely stopped the wars that exposed failures.
